meta.title: Who really said "If voting changed anything, they'd make it illegal"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Not Emma Goldman. First documented in 1976, 36 years after her death — an anonymous anarchist slogan recorded as graffiti. Here is the paper trail.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'If voting changed anything, they'd make it illegal'?
meta.ogDescription: Emma Goldman didn't say it. The line surfaces in 1976 as an anonymous protest slogan and graffiti — and only reaches her name decades later.

answer.label: Not Emma Goldman — an anonymous protest slogan
answer.authorDates: Earliest documented 1976 · circulated as anti-electoral graffiti
answer.sourceLine: Emma Goldman died in 1940, and this saying is not documented anywhere until 1976; it appears in none of her published writings or recorded speeches. Researchers trace it instead to anonymous anti-electoral sloganeering — it was logged in print as graffiti years before any named person was ever credited with it.

source.excerpt: If voting could change anything, it would be illegal; when it threatens to change anything, it becomes illegal.
trail: Quote researcher Barry Popik’s file on the saying ↗ — posted 30 June 2010 and, as the entry itself states, “prepared with the assistance of Garson O’Toole, the Quote Investigator” — gives its earliest dated instance as North Country Anvil, May–June 1976, with no author attached. Goldman’s name does not appear anywhere in that chronology until a 2007 anthology.

Wikiquote files the line in its Disputed section ↗, noting that “although often attributed to Goldman, there is no evidence that she made such a statement,” and pointing to a 24 September 1976 letter by Robert S. Borden in the Lowell, Massachusetts Sun as the earliest known example.

Matt Seybold’s investigation for the Center for Mark Twain Studies ↗ reaches the same verdict from the other direction: the aphorism “is not present in her many published writings and recorded speeches.” He quotes Charles Umney’s Class Matters (2018) calling it “an old anarchist slogan, frequently found as lamp-post graffiti in university cities.”

What Goldman did argue about the ballot is in “Woman Suffrage,” collected in Anarchism and Other Essays (1910) ↗, where she calls universal suffrage “our modern fetich” — a different sentence making a different point, and the one she actually put in print.
source.excerptNote: The earliest dated instance in Barry Popik’s file, from North Country Anvil (May–June 1976), where it carries no author. The now-familiar “they’d make it illegal” wording is logged later, and always as street writing: Jonathon Green’s The Cynic’s Lexicon (1984) lists it under GRAFFITI, dated London, 1979, and Mother Jones in April 1982 wrote, “The graffiti that says, ‘If voting changed anything, they’d make it illegal’ just about sums it up.”

sourceLink.text: Barry Popik’s dated chronology of the saying

source.rightsNote: The wording has no identified author: its earliest dated appearance is 1976, and every source that traces it records it as an anonymous slogan or graffiti, so no copyright status can honestly be asserted for it. Goldman’s own Anarchism and Other Essays (1910) is long in the public domain in the United States — but this line is not in it.

author.name: Emma Goldman
author.kicker: About the woman it gets pinned on
author.heading: What Emma Goldman actually argued
author.bio: Emma Goldman was a Russian-born anarchist revolutionary, political activist and writer, born 27 June 1869 and died 14 May 1940. She published Anarchism and Other Essays in 1910, and deliberately distanced herself from first-wave feminism and its campaign for the vote. Her essay “Woman Suffrage” calls universal suffrage “our modern fetich” and argues that it “has only helped to enslave people” — a real and genuinely unpopular position, which is exactly why a punchier modern slogan keeps getting mistaken for hers.

Not found in Emma Goldman, Anarchism and Other Essays (New York, 1910).

copyAttribution: "If voting changed anything, they'd make it illegal." — Not Emma Goldman. The saying has no known author: its earliest documented appearance is May–June 1976, in North Country Anvil, as "If voting could change anything, it would be illegal," and it was recorded through the late 1970s and 1980s as anonymous anarchist graffiti. Goldman died in 1940 and the line appears in none of her published writings. Via Quotle.info.

misattribution.heading: Who it gets credited to, and why none of it holds
misattribution.intro: This is one of the internet’s most durable orphan quotes: a line with no author that keeps being handed to whichever dead radical suits the politics of whoever is sharing it.

items.why: Goldman died on 14 May 1940 — thirty-six years before the saying’s earliest documented appearance. Wikiquote files it under Disputed ↗ with the note that “although often attributed to Goldman, there is no evidence that she made such a statement,” and the Jewish Women’s Archive ↗ says flatly that “there’s no evidence either one of them ever committed that quote to print.”

The Center for Mark Twain Studies ↗ traces the Twain version to social media specifically: Matt Seybold found “no instance of it being associated with Twain prior to” a tweet on Election Day 2008, after which a handful of accounts recycled it daily until it stuck.

items.who: Philip Berrigan, Travus T. Hipp, Bob Avakian
items.why: Seybold lists all three ↗: Daniel Berrigan named his brother Philip in a 2008 Nation interview; two Reno Gazette-Journal stories called it a “typical motto” of broadcaster Travus T. Hipp; and the revised And I Quote (2003) credits Bob Avakian. Seybold could not find the line in Hipp’s or Avakian’s accessible writings.

Livingstone’s memoir is titled If voting changed anything, they’d abolish it ↗ (Collins, 1987) — but three years earlier, in Who’s Afraid of Margaret Thatcher? (1984), he had introduced the line as “a slogan I have occasionally seen painted on walls, I think by anarchists at the time of elections,” as Popik’s file records ↗. He borrowed it; he did not coin it.

misattribution.truthLine: The honest answer is that nobody knows who said it first. Popik’s chronology ↗ runs from an unsigned 1976 magazine line, through a decade of graffiti sightings, to a 2007 anthology that finally set Emma Goldman’s name beside it. The credit arrived last, not first.

context.heading: Why it sticks to her
lead: Goldman really was an anti-voting radical, which is precisely why the slogan slides onto her name without resistance. In “Woman Suffrage,” collected in Anarchism and Other Essays (1910), she wrote that “our modern fetich is universal suffrage,” and that women had not yet seen “that suffrage is an evil, that it has only helped to enslave people, that it has but closed their eyes that they may not see how craftily they were made to submit.”

But her argument is not the slogan’s argument. Goldman says the ballot is a false idol that pacifies the people who hold it — a critique of what voters believe about themselves. The slogan says the powerful would outlaw voting if it ever worked — a conspiracy joke about what the powerful are up to. The second one fits on a wall, which is exactly where it was first written down.
context.detailsSummary: How the wording drifted, decade by decade
detailsBody: May–June 1976 — North Country Anvil, p. 136: “If voting could change anything, it would be illegal; when it threatens to change anything, it becomes illegal.” No author given.
24 September 1976 — a letter to the Lowell, Massachusetts Sun from Robert S. Borden: “If voting could change anything it would be made illegal!”
1979 — the Yale Book of Quotations (2006) files the saying under “Sayings” and cites Rennie Ellis, Australian Graffiti Revisited (1979): “If voting could change things, it would be illegal.”
April 1982 — Mother Jones: “The graffiti that says, ‘If voting changed anything, they’d make it illegal’ just about sums it up.”
1984 — Jonathon Green’s The Cynic’s Lexicon lists the modern wording under GRAFFITI, dated London, 1979.
2007 — Jon Winokur’s The Big Curmudgeon, p. 623, prints it with the byline EMMA GOLDMAN — the first time her name appears beside it in Popik’s file.
context.pull: Our modern fetich is universal suffrage.

sourcesVerified.claim: Popik's entry (posted 30 June 2010, "prepared with the assistance of Garson O'Toole, the Quote Investigator") gives the earliest dated instance as North Country Anvil, vols. 18-25, May-June 1976, p. 136; the 24 Sept 1976 Lowell Sun letter by Robert S. Borden; Mother Jones April 1982 calling it graffiti; Jonathon Green's The Cynic's Lexicon (1984) listing it under GRAFFITI, London, 1979; Tariq Ali & Ken Livingstone, Who's Afraid of Margaret Thatcher? (1984) p. 93 calling it a wall slogan seen 'by anarchists at the time of elections'; Yale Book of Quotations (2006) p. 668 citing Rennie Ellis, Australian Graffiti Revisited (1979); and Jon Winokur, The Big Curmudgeon (2007), p. 623 crediting EMMA GOLDMAN.

Wikiquote's Emma Goldman page lists the line in its 'Disputed' section with the note 'Although often attributed to Goldman, there is no evidence that she made such a statement,' names the 24 September 1976 Lowell Sun piece by Robert S. Borden as the earliest known example, lists variants including 'If voting changed anything, they'd make it illegal,' and notes Mark Twain and Philip Berrigan are also incorrectly credited.

Matt Seybold, Center for Mark Twain Studies: the aphorism 'is not present in her many published writings and recorded speeches'; quotes Charles Umney's Class Matters (2018) calling it 'an old anarchist slogan, frequently found as lamp-post graffiti in university cities'; found 'no instance of it being associated with Twain prior to' an Election Day 2008 tweet; and lists Philip Berrigan (via Daniel Berrigan's 2008 Nation interview), Travus T. Hipp (Reno Gazette-Journal, 'typical motto') and Bob Avakian (And I Quote, 2003) as rival claimants he could not confirm in their accessible writings.

Project Gutenberg's edition of Emma Goldman's Anarchism and Other Essays contains the essay 'Woman Suffrage' with the sentences 'Our modern fetich is universal suffrage' and 'suffrage is an evil, that it has only helped to enslave people, that it has but closed their eyes that they may not see how craftily they were made to submit'; the preface is dated 'New York, December, 1910'; the ebook page states the work is public domain in the USA and dates it 1910. Full-text search of the book returns no instance of the slogan.

Jewish Women's Archive: 'Sometimes it's attributed to Mark Twain, but usually Emma Goldman is cited as the source. (For the record, there's no evidence either one of them ever committed that quote to print.)' The article also quotes Goldman's essay 'Woman Suffrage' and describes her anarchist case against the ballot.
Open Library work record confirms 'If voting changed anything, they'd abolish it' by Ken Livingstone, first published 1987, published by Collins in 1987 with a Fontana edition in 1988.
